job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Elena Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in robotics at Lindau Technical College, and I share a flat above a bakery with a friend from my course. In the day I'm in the robotics lab teaching a robot arm to sort recycling by touch, which was also my final bachelor's project in mechatronics. In the evening I code, usually with an AI assistant that drafts and explains things, and I read about funding rounds for robotics firms because I'm a bit obsessed. I finished top of my class, with internships at a warehouse robotics company and at a hospital supply lab. My mum is a school secretary and raised me alone, so I try not to cost her anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a fair summary of the last two years. The tools are handy for drafts and tests, but they don't solve the hard problems. In my field I'd say robots are still slow and fiddly, which is why people like me exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it makes me a bit uneasy, and it's not what you'd expect. Robotics start-ups live on hype money, and if the story goes cold, funding dries up and hiring freezes. I'd still be able to get a job, but fewer of the exciting ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and apply to the warehouse robotics company and two industrial automation firms, which have steadier customers. I'd keep using the AI assistant for drafts, as I do now. I'd put 150 a month into savings and not spend any of my mum's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not worried. It's a risk for my field, not a disaster for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a surprise, that no big change would worry you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of the money in robotics is a bet that things change. If they don't, the bet loses. I'd rather have a boring factory automation job than a start-up that folds in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a start-up offered you more but a factory firm offered you safety?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the safe one first and do the start-up on weekends. My mum worked hard so I don't have to gamble, and I take that seriously.

say: The tools are **handy**, but they don't solve the hard problems, and robots are still slow.
That's what people like me are for.
think: Robotics start-ups live on **hype money**, so a plateau could freeze hiring.
I'd still find a job, but fewer **exciting** ones.
do: Apply to the warehouse robotics firm and two **industrial automation** firms.
Keep using the AI assistant for **drafts**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but it's a risk for my field, not a disaster for me.
S0.quote: A lot of the money in robotics is a bet that things change. If they don't, the bet loses.
fieldNote: Elena's unease comes from a **surprising direction**: her field depends on the story of change, so a plateau threatens her sector.
She puts her mother's **sacrifice** ahead of risk-taking when choosing a first job.

steps.text: Apply to the warehouse robotics firm and two industrial automation firms
Put 150 a month into a savings account
Keep using the AI assistant for code drafts and tests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, this is where things get interesting. Software will take over a lot of thinking tasks, and robots will follow slowly, which means someone has to connect the two. I'd tell friends to learn a bit of both coding and mechanics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm well placed. I can code with the tools and understand the hardware, which not many people can. I'd worry about my friends from pure software, because their kind of job is the one that shrinks first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for a mixed role in automation, where I use AI to plan and test robot behaviour. I'd write a small open-source tool for tuning robot grips, because a public project looks good to employers. I'd also use my university contacts to get a friend, Sophie, an interview at the warehouse company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pleased, honestly. Some nerves, but the good kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said pure software friends are exposed. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sophie (a friend from her course) does web development, and the internship she did was mostly writing the same pages over and over. She's smart but her tasks are the first to go, and she knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something that could go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the hardware side moves faster than expected, or if one big firm takes the whole market. Then I'm just another engineer waiting for a call.

say: This is where it gets **interesting**: software takes thinking tasks and someone must connect it to robots.
I'd tell friends to learn **coding and mechanics**.
think: I'm **well placed**, because I can code with the tools and understand hardware.
Friends in pure software are **more exposed** than me.
do: Aim for a mixed **automation** role using AI to test robot behaviour.
Write a small open-source tool for tuning robot **grips**.
Get a friend an **interview** through my contacts.
feel: **Pleased**, with nerves of the good kind.
S1.quote: Sophie (a friend from her course) does web development, and the internship she did was mostly writing the same pages over and over.
fieldNote: Elena sees **two sides** of AI: it is an opportunity for her and a threat for pure-software peers.
She is already planning to help a **friend** through her contacts, which shows a collaborative style.

steps.text: Apply for automation roles that combine AI testing and robot hardware
Publish an open-source tool for tuning robot grips
Use AI tools to plan and test robot behaviour in my thesis
Ask my contacts at the warehouse firm to interview my friend Sophie

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say wow, in a nervous voice. I'd tell people this is bigger than anyone can plan for and that governments need to act on income support and retraining now. I'd also say that robots in 2031 mean this is not just an office story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm more worried than I let on. I'm not as safe as I thought, because the AI could do most of the design work and the robots take the hands-on work from 2031. My own field is the one that gets built the fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job as soon as possible, preferably in robot deployment, where a human still installs and checks robots in real buildings. I'd cut my spending to rent and food and save about 500 a month if I get a salary. And I'd talk to my mum about her job at the school, because office work there is easy to automate, and I want her to have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, wobbly. I'd take it step by step and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be more worried than you let on. What do you hide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From my mum I hide that I think her job is exposed too. From my course friends I hide that I don't know what a robotics engineer does when the AI designs the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is it about deployment work that you trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It happens in a room full of messy real life. A factory has a broken pallet, a wet floor, a worker who stands in the wrong place. That's not a clean problem.

Robots in 2031 mean this isn't just an **office story**.
think: I'm **less safe** than I thought, because AI could do most design work.
My own field is the one that gets **built** fastest.
do: Take a **robot deployment** job as soon as possible.
Cut spending to rent and food and save **500 a month**.
Talk to my mum about **her job** at the school.
feel: **Uneasy** and wobbly, taking it step by step.
S2.quote: A factory has a broken pallet, a wet floor, a worker who stands in the wrong place. That's not a clean problem.
fieldNote: Elena is the **most adaptive** person here, yet admits her field is built fastest by the very technology.
She hides her fear for her **mother's job** from her mother, which shows the weight she carries.

steps.text: Take a robot deployment job at a warehouse firm within three months
Cut spending to rent and food only
Save 500 a month from the first salary
Sit down with my mum and plan for her school office job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a real chance. I'd say let's build robots people trust and make rules about who benefits. I'd tell people to start learning and save cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. By 2031 I'd be 29 with five years of deployment experience, and I'd be the person who knows how the machines fail. That's useful when robots arrive in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first automation job, then specialise in safety and testing, because someone has to prove robots are safe. I'd save about 400 a month and pay off my loan, about 7,500. I'd keep learning from the AI tools daily, because that's where I'd get my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It's a real chance to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years does not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me get hands-on stories, like which sensor lies and which gripper breaks. Two years leaves me with ideas and no scars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots arrive faster than expected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be near the front and could work on safety. I'd rather be in the room than reading about it.

say: Five years gives us a **real chance** to build robots people trust.
think: By 2031 I'd have **five years** of deployment experience and know how machines fail.
do: Take the first automation job, then specialise in **safety** and testing.
Save **400 a month** and pay off the 7,500 loan.
Keep learning from the **AI tools** daily.
feel: **Calm** and curious, because it's a real chance to be useful.
S3.quote: Five years lets me get hands-on stories, like which sensor lies and which gripper breaks. Two years leaves me with ideas and no scars.
fieldNote: Elena thinks in terms of **experience and scars**, which is why five years feels so different from two.
She plans to move into **robot safety** and testing, a role she says someone must fill.

steps.text: Take the first automation job and ask for field deployment work
Specialise in robot safety testing through a certificate course
Save 400 a month and pay off the 7,500 loan
Use an AI assistant daily to review test plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and that robotics should be the part we get right. I'd tell people not to fear it, and to learn at their own speed. I'd also want a better plan for how people share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm and quite excited. By 2036 I'd be 34, maybe leading a small team, maybe with a child. The hands-on robots come around 2039, so I'd be in the middle of building them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a deployment role, then move into design and safety within five years. I'd save 500 a month, and buy a small flat. And I'd put time into teaching teenagers about robots, because I love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and really quite happy. It's the nicest of the five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody makes a plan, because it's so far away. I've seen how ten years of drift looks, in my mum's school. Slow change can be as hard as fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about teaching teenagers.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I help run a robot club on Thursdays. A fifteen-year-old made a robot water my mum's plants last month. That's what I want to do more of.

say: Ten years is a **lot of time**, so robotics is the part we should get right.
People should learn at their **own speed** and not fear it.
think: I'd be **calm** and excited, maybe leading a small team by 2036.
I'd be in the middle of **building robots** when they arrive.
do: Finish the master's and take a **deployment role**.
Move into design and **safety** within five years.
Save **500 a month** and buy a small flat.
S4.quote: I've seen how ten years of drift looks, in my mum's school. Slow change can be as hard as fast.
fieldNote: Elena is **most at ease** here, picturing a team and a child, though she names slow drift as a real risk.
Her robot club shows she wants to **spread** the skills, not hoard them.

steps.text: Save 500 a month towards a small flat
Plan a family around a steady engineering job by 34
Move from deployment into robot design and safety within five years
Keep running the Thursday robot club for teenagers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it removes the time to get experience before robots arrive. What would help is wage support while people retrain, and good public information about which jobs will stay human the longest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm the confident one in my family and I'm scared my mum is the one who'll be hurt. I'd like to build something that makes her work easier, not take it away.

headlineQuote: I'm the confident one in my family and I'm scared my mum is the one who'll be hurt.
portrait: Elena is a 24-year-old **mechatronics** graduate doing a master's in robotics, raised by her mother, a school secretary.
She uses AI tools every day, sits politically in the middle and is **adaptive**, curious and a bit obsessed with her field.
Her surprise is that a plateau worries her more than most, because robotics money lives on **hype**.
She sees fast change as a chance, but fears most for her **mother's job** and her pure-software friends.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it removes the time to gain experience before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Wage support** during retraining and clear public information about which jobs stay human longest.
